The two-homes trap this key used to warn about is now closed by having ONE key rather than one-per-CLI; the `_why` and `_first_reading` notes below are HISTORY of the superseded design, kept because their measurements still frame what the merged hint is and is not doing.
hints.mcp_fallback:
## If a page will not open

You have MCP tools available in this session for reading web pages, and they are usually stronger than a plain fetch. When a page returns 403, 404, a CAPTCHA, a Cloudflare interstitial, an empty body or a JavaScript-only shell, do NOT give up and do NOT answer from memory. Look at the MCP tools you have available RIGHT NOW - some CLIs load tools lazily and you must issue a tool search first before you can see them - and try whichever one fits the failure. Say in your answer which tool finally worked.

Do NOT fetch or parse a page with the shell (`curl`, `wget`, `python -c`, one-off scripts) unless you have already verified the shell works in this environment. On many CLIs the shell path is either denied by policy (in which case one denied call may discard the whole run) or unable to spawn a subprocess at all - either way, a shell attempt in those cases costs you the run without returning a page. The MCP tools do not go through the shell.

Do NOT use billing-heavy fetchers - anything that bills per page or per token with no ceiling. Prefer free tools; use a metered scrape only as a last resort for a single page. If your session offers a whole-site crawler or an unbounded page-extraction agent, treat those as the meter you are asked to avoid, whatever they are named.

If everything fails, write that the page could not be opened, name what you tried, and tag the claim `[SNIPPET]` or `my search found no confirmation`. A host that refuses automated traffic has given an answer; do not try to defeat it.
hints._generalised_2026_08_08: 🔴 2026-08-08, the operator: «просто скажи, что бы он использовал MCP, а какие именно, не надо, ведь какой-то MCP мог зависнуть и в этот момент не загрузился». Sharper than the earlier «one CLI's tool list differs from another's» that had two paragraphs living where one should have. Availability is DYNAMIC, not static: a server present at install time can be hung, unloaded or filtered out by permissions when the actual call happens - and a named-but-absent tool makes the model report OUR error as its own. That is the same trap that produced the 2026-08-08 morning `NONE` reading for codex, one layer down. The two old paragraphs (`agy_mcp_fallback`, `codex_mcp_fallback`) are GONE; their measurement history is preserved in the `_why` and `_first_reading` notes below, and those notes are now archaeology - the current hint is `mcp_fallback` above, and it names ZERO tools. hints._codex_mcp_fallback_why: 🔴 SUPERSEDED 2026-08-08 by the merger noted above - kept because the CODE OF THE HINT is gone but the MEASUREMENTS are still true and still frame what the merged hint means. 🔴🔴 SUPERSEDES THE 2026-08-08 MORNING CONCLUSION THAT CODEX HAS NO MCP TOOLS. That conclusion came from asking the model («name your MCP page-reading tools») and taking `NONE` as a measurement. It was wrong, and the cause is worth more than the correction: codex-cli 0.147 loads tools LAZILY - the model sees them only after issuing a `tool_search_call` - so «what tools do you have?» is answered from an empty list unless it searches first. Asking a model to enumerate its own tools measures its discovery behaviour, not its tool set. RE-MEASURED the same day, by execution and by the client's own event log rather than by the model's word: `codex mcp list --json` reports NINE configured servers, all `enabled: true`; a probe run produced `mcp_tool_call_end {server: scrapling, tool: fetch}` -> `Ok`, and a second produced `{server: crawl4ai, tool: crawl_url}` -> `Ok`, both returning the real `<h1>` of example.com. 🔴 THE FIRST RE-PROBE WAS ALSO WRONG, in the same direction: after ONE tool search the model reported 3 servers / 20 tools and stated that jina «does not expose read_url». After eleven searches it reported 10 namespaces and 51 tools INCLUDING `read_url` - the first number was the search's `limit`, not the machine's. So even a probe that calls a tool successfully can enumerate the rest wrongly; the enumeration is a self-report at every depth, and only the `mcp_tool_call_end` frames are evidence. That is why the merged hint's first paragraph is about searching rather than about any particular tool. 🔴 Codex also carries `mcp__codex_apps__*` servers (github, tavily_ai, sites) that are NOT in ~/.codex/config.toml - vendor-side apps. They are deliberately not named in the hint: they were seen once, in one model's enumeration, which by the paragraph above is not evidence.
hints._agy_mcp_fallback_why: 🔴 SUPERSEDED 2026-08-08 by the merger noted above - kept for the anti-shell measurement, which is the paragraph the merged hint still carries. 2026-08-08, the operator: «может agy и codex писать доп. текст в промт, что бы они использовали MCP разные для открытия сайтов, если их встроенный fetch не смог открыть сайт?» — YES for agy, and 🔴 YES FOR CODEX TOO since the re-measurement recorded in `_codex_mcp_fallback_why` (the first answer here said NO, on the strength of the model's own `NONE`; that was a self-report, not a measurement, and it was wrong). The old two hints stayed SEPARATE rather than shared because tool names differed, the discovery model differed and the anti-shell paragraph had a different CAUSE on each (agy: a denied command discards the whole run; codex: the sandboxed shell cannot spawn PowerShell at all). 🔴 The 2026-08-08 evening merger reversed that: names dropped, generic wording covers both discovery paths, and the anti-shell paragraph covers both causes in one sentence («denied by policy OR unable to spawn») because dodging shell is the right advice under either. 🔴 The six servers named in the old agy hint were read from ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/mcp.json, not recalled: scrapling, playwright, firecrawl, jina-mcp-server, crawl4ai, cloakbrowser. 🔴 THE ANTI-SHELL PARAGRAPH IS THE REAL PAYLOAD, and it is aimed at a measured failure, not at a hypothetical one: round 27 watched agy die THREE times on three DIFFERENT one-off `python -c` scripts, each denied, each discarding a run that had already made ~29 successful tool calls. The failure is the deep-researcher profile's habit of shelling a fresh script, not a missing page. 🔴 It also goes WITH the grain of a measurement already in this repo: an earlier instruction telling agy to AVOID MCP failed 5/5, because a server's own tool description outranks a system prompt. Pointing it AT the tools it is already pulled toward pushes the same lever the way it already moves - which is why this one is worth trying and that one was not. 🔴 Firecrawl is named ONLY to forbid the unbounded call: the operator's spend policy is enforced by a Claude Code PreToolUse hook, and that hook does not cover agy's own MCP client.
hints._first_reading_2026_08_08: 🟢 FIRST READING, CONSISTENT WITH THE HYPOTHESIS - and it is one reading, not a proof. Round 28, both agy channels, counted from their own stream-json: agy31pro used 2 tools (both search_web); agy36flash used 14 (6 search_web, 4 view_file, 4 call_mcp_tool). `run_command` count: ZERO on both, and both returned status SUCCESS with a full answer - where round 27 had every attempt die on a denied one-off `python -c`. 🔴 WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH, and the distinction is the whole point: THE BRIEF CHANGED TOO. Round 27's brief was about packages and registries and provoked scripted downloads; round 28's was a design review that did not. Two variables moved, so the honest claim is «no shelling occurred and MCP was used four times», never «the hint prevented shelling». Isolating it costs one round: re-run round 27's brief WITH the hint. Do that before trusting this paragraph. 🔴 It does already correct round 27's other conclusion, that «agy31pro is unusable headless» - it ran fine here, so the failure was never the model.

groups._doc: A word a human types that means SEVERAL channels. Without these, splitting agy into two channels would have broken `--only agy` and «не используй gemini» with 'unknown channel' - the exact defect that made `--only http` unusable for weeks in 2026-07. A group is expanded by routing before anything else runs, so every flag and every free-text route accepts it. Group names and their aliases share one namespace with channel and model aliases, and a collision is refused at load time.

Same lesson as the agy toolset fence: a reviewer needs the public web and nothing else, and the restriction must be mechanical rather than written in the brief.
fetch_tool._budget: max_calls is a CEILING, not a target. When it is reached the model is TOLD so through a tool result and asked to answer from what it has; silently dropping an unanswered tool call leaves it waiting for a result that never arrives, and the observed outcome of that is an empty answer with no end marker. goog36flash._title_is_the_publisher: 🟢 FREE AND PREVIOUSLY DISCARDED. So the sources are often nameable with zero extra requests. The parser guards the SHAPE rather than trusting the field, because `title` is documented only as a display string and naming a publisher we cannot name would be the same failure pointing the other way. 🔴 «Usually» is measured, not hedging: a later run on the same channel returned 4 annotations whose titles the guard rejected, and another returned foxsports.com + uefa.com cleanly. Whether a single-user citation audit is «another purpose» is arguable (the terms contemplate displaying results to the end user who submitted the prompt, which is exactly this tool), but the kit is PUBLIC and a default is what strangers run. So: publisher DOMAINS on by default (no request, nothing followed); FOLLOWING the Links off by default, behind --resolve-grounding-links. deep._what_it_is: More TIME, more READING, more ROOM TO THINK - deliberately not «more effort», because on four of the seven vendors strategic is already at the ceiling and there is nowhere above it.
